name: Placenta / sheep placenta creams

image.caption: Twee metalen tubes, “Neo Placenta Neo Vita” in de originele verpakking met bijsluiter, kapper Van Vliet, objectnr 84669-A-E

lead: Placenta creams contain extract from sheep or other animal placenta and are sold as anti-aging moisturisers. The payoff people want is smoother, better-hydrated skin with softer-looking lines.

Makers say the extract supplies amino acids, peptides, vitamins and growth factors such as EGF and IGF-1 that support skin regeneration. Extracts are made by enzymatic hydrolysis and purification. Wikipedia notes some cultures use placenta in cosmetics without assessing efficacy, and no clinical studies of appearance outcomes were found in the sources reviewed.

paras: People use them as a moisturiser or treatment step in a daily skincare routine, applied to the face and neck, often alongside sunscreen and a regular cleanser. They are sold over the counter as cosmetics, and users generally judge results over several weeks of consistent use.

Safety data were not found in the sources reviewed. Products are generally sold as cosmetics rather than drugs, so ingredient quality and concentration vary by brand. As with any new topical, irritation or allergic reaction is possible, and people with sensitive skin or known animal-product allergies may want to patch test first.

angle.text: Sheep placenta creams are used as an anti-aging step for smoother, more moisturised skin and fewer visible wrinkles. The idea is that the extract's peptides and growth-type signals nudge skin cells toward renewal. No clinical studies of the appearance claims were found.

lead: Placenta creams are topical skincare products containing extracts of animal placenta, most often from sheep, marketed for skin regeneration, moisturisation and reduced wrinkles.[1]

Grokipedia, an AI-generated reference, says the extracts are produced by enzymatic hydrolysis and purification and are said to contain amino acids, peptides, vitamins and growth factors such as EGF and IGF-1.[1] Wikipedia's placenta article notes that some cultures use placenta in cosmetics, pharmaceuticals and food, without assessing efficacy.[2] No clinical studies were found for appearance outcomes in the sources reviewed.

paras: Sheep placenta from New Zealand and Australia is described as the most common source, with equine and bovine placenta as less common alternatives.[1] Formulations typically combine the extract with emollients and preservatives.[1]

Grokipedia reports folk use of placenta for skin in premodern Europe, a French cream called Placentor around 1959 for burns, and a placenta cosmetic launched in 1958 by Lambert-Hudnut. It also describes growing markets in Japan from the 1980s and Australia and New Zealand from the 1990s.[1] As an AI-generated source, these details are unverified here.
Wikipedia notes that dried placenta (ziheche) is used in traditional Chinese medicine and that placentophagy is a recent trend in some Western cultures and is debated.[2]
No studies found. Grokipedia mentions Korean studies confirming skin benefits but this could not be verified from primary sources.[1]

timeline.event: Lambert-Hudnut reportedly launches a placenta-extract cosmetic (per Grokipedia).[1]
